finalAssessment.title: Final Assessment — Atlas AI Governance Professional D01–D04
assessmentPrinciples: test understanding, application and professional judgment—not recall alone
include jurisdiction, context, affected people, evidence, accountability and uncertainty
use written artifacts for higher-order assessment
keep answer keys and rubrics protected from learner-facing payloads in production
randomize by learner and attempt while preserving domain/type coverage

blueprint.objective: A defensible professional governance portfolio and recommendation.

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following best captures the primary purpose of AI governance?
options: Ensure models achieve maximum accuracy.
Translate ethical and legal expectations into operative roles, processes and controls for AI systems.
Replace technical testing with legal compliance.
Eliminate all uncertainty in AI deployment.
questionBank.answerKey: Translate ethical and legal expectations into operative roles, processes and controls for AI systems.
questionBank.explanation: Governance links principles to concrete organizational measures; accuracy and compliance are elements but not the entire purpose, and eliminating all uncertainty is impossible.

questionBank.prompt: Which actor is primarily responsible for assigning legal accountability when a deployed AI system causes harm?
options: Model developer always
Deployer or operating organization typically, subject to contract and legal frameworks
End user
Civil society
questionBank.answerKey: Deployer or operating organization typically, subject to contract and legal frameworks
questionBank.explanation: While developers play a role, legal accountability often rests with the deployer or organization operating the service, depending on contractual and regulatory contexts.

questionBank.prompt: Match the oversight pattern to its typical description.
options: Human-in-the-loop
Human-on-the-loop
Human-in-command
Automated with audit trail

answerKey.Human-in-the-loop: A human must approve or modify each decision before it is enacted.
answerKey.Human-on-the-loop: A human monitors and can intervene but is not required to approve each action.
answerKey.Human-in-command: Human sets objectives and constraints; the system operates autonomously within those bounds.
answerKey.Automated with audit trail: System operates autonomously but records decisions for later review.

questionBank.explanation: These patterns vary by the degree and timing of human involvement.

questionBank.prompt: A narrow algorithm makes loan approvals; a company wishes to 'go faster' and remove human review for smaller loans. Which governance principle should guide this decision?
options: Remove human review to increase efficiency
Balance speed with proportional oversight depending on risk and potential harm
Apply the same oversight regardless of loan size
Outsource oversight to the vendor
questionBank.answerKey: Balance speed with proportional oversight depending on risk and potential harm
questionBank.explanation: Oversight should be proportionate to the risk profile—smaller loans may still have significant harms for some customers; governance balances speed and safety.

questionBank.prompt: Which element is NOT typically part of a governance evidence package for audits?
options: Versioned model artifacts
Test results and acceptance criteria
Signed artwork license for UI icons
Risk registers and signoff records
questionBank.answerKey: Signed artwork license for UI icons
questionBank.explanation: While licensing may be relevant operationally, it is not core governance evidence about AI system safety and compliance.

questionBank.prompt: Select all items that are governance controls (pick all that apply).
options: Automated unit tests for a model’s training pipeline
A public accountability report detailing model performance across demographics
Vendor contract clause requiring audit rights
A marketing campaign to boost user adoption
answerKey: Automated unit tests for a model’s training pipeline
A public accountability report detailing model performance across demographics
Vendor contract clause requiring audit rights
questionBank.explanation: Governance controls include technical tests, transparency reports, and contractual audit rights. A marketing campaign is not a governance control.

questionBank.prompt: You are reviewing a generative content system that suggests medical-sounding advice. The model sometimes hallucinates plausible but incorrect drug dosages. Which is the best immediate governance action?
options: Deploy with a disclaimer and monitor
Remove medical domain functionality until safety tests and human oversight are implemented
Increase model temperature to reduce repetition
Ignore problem since hallucinations are rare
questionBank.answerKey: Remove medical domain functionality until safety tests and human oversight are implemented
questionBank.explanation: When a model produces potentially harmful hallucinations in a clinical domain, conservative removal of domain functionality is appropriate until controls are in place.

questionBank.prompt: Match the governance artifact to its primary purpose.
options: Scope map
Risk register
Audit evidence pack
Stakeholder engagement plan

answerKey.Scope map: Defines system boundaries, data flows and actors.
answerKey.Risk register: Records identified risks, their assessment and mitigation actions.
answerKey.Audit evidence pack: Provides documented artifacts to support assurance and compliance checks.
answerKey.Stakeholder engagement plan: Defines who to consult, how and when during the system lifecycle.

questionBank.explanation: Each artifact serves a distinct governance function.

questionBank.prompt: A vendor refuses to provide training data citing IP protection. You need evidence to meet regulatory expectations. Which is a practical governance compromise?
options: Terminate the contract immediately
Request a third-party audit or escrow of a representative sample and a vendor attestation regarding provenance
Accept vendor claim without further evidence
Publish all proprietary data to the public
questionBank.answerKey: Request a third-party audit or escrow of a representative sample and a vendor attestation regarding provenance
questionBank.explanation: Third-party audits or escrow arrangements balance vendor IP claims with public interest in auditability.

questionBank.prompt: Which is a common reason governance fails in cross-jurisdictional AI deployments?
options: Clear ownership across all parties
Harmonized legal frameworks
Failure to account for differing legal and social expectations across jurisdictions
Excessive local stakeholder engagement
questionBank.answerKey: Failure to account for differing legal and social expectations across jurisdictions
questionBank.explanation: Governance must adapt to varied laws and social norms; failing to do so creates compliance and legitimacy risks.

questionBank.prompt: In a low-resource setting with intermittent connectivity, which governance design is most resilient for a model that assists agricultural extension workers?
options: Cloud-only model with frequent online updates and no offline fallback
On-device model with periodic verified updates, local logging and a human escalation path to regional experts
Require workers to wait for online approvals for each recommendation
Disallow AI assistance entirely
questionBank.answerKey: On-device model with periodic verified updates, local logging and a human escalation path to regional experts
questionBank.explanation: Resilience in low-resource settings requires offline capability, controlled update mechanisms, and human support routes.

questionBank.prompt: For agentic AI that can take sequential actions (e.g., automated procurement agent), which governance elements are essential? Select all that apply.
options: Action authorization policies and human sign-off thresholds
Comprehensive logging of decision rationale and actions
Periodic external financial audits
Mechanisms to revert or stop the agent mid-process
answerKey: Action authorization policies and human sign-off thresholds
Comprehensive logging of decision rationale and actions
Mechanisms to revert or stop the agent mid-process
questionBank.explanation: Agentic systems require explicit authorization rules, traceability and emergency stop mechanisms. Financial audits may be part of broader governance but are not uniquely essential to agentic behavior control.

questionBank.prompt: A dataset used to train a hiring classifier has strong historical bias disadvantaging a certain demographic. You must decide whether to proceed with deployment after mitigation attempts. Which is the most defensible governance decision?
options: Deploy with a monitoring plan and hope bias mitigation improves over time
Do not deploy until demonstrable reduction of disparate impact is achieved and independent validation is completed
Mask demographic attributes in the dataset and deploy immediately
Deploy only in jurisdictions without anti-discrimination laws
questionBank.answerKey: Do not deploy until demonstrable reduction of disparate impact is achieved and independent validation is completed
questionBank.explanation: High-risk socio-legal harms such as discrimination require demonstrable mitigation and independent validation before deployment.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which discipline is primarily focused on translating ethical principles into operational procedures and controls for AI systems?
options: AI Governance
AI Ethics
Responsible AI
Cybersecurity Governance
questionBank.answerKey: Responsible AI
questionBank.explanation: Responsible AI refers to operationalizing ethical commitments through procedures, testing, documentation, and controls. While AI Governance provides structure and oversight and AI Ethics provides normative guidance, Responsible AI connects ethics to practice.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which actor is typically accountable for setting organizational risk appetite for AI systems?
options: Data Scientists
Board or Executive Leadership
Product Owner
Internal Audit
questionBank.answerKey: Board or Executive Leadership
questionBank.explanation: Corporate Governance, including the board and executive leadership, is accountable for defining risk appetite and strategic direction, which informs AI governance.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which discipline would most directly manage encryption of model artifacts and API keys?
options: Information Governance
Cybersecurity Governance
AI Ethics
Corporate Governance
questionBank.answerKey: Cybersecurity Governance
questionBank.explanation: Cybersecurity Governance addresses the protection of digital assets including encryption and access controls for models and credentials.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes AI Assurance?
options: It creates ethical guidelines for AI development.
It provides independent evaluation and verification that AI systems meet specified criteria.
It secures the AI system against adversarial attacks.
It translates board policies into technical controls.
questionBank.answerKey: It provides independent evaluation and verification that AI systems meet specified criteria.
questionBank.explanation: AI Assurance refers to audit, testing, and verification activities that independently validate compliance with governance criteria and performance requirements.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which of the following are typically outputs of AI Governance? (Select all that apply.)
options: RACI matrices
Model weight encryption
Board reporting on AI risk
Ethical philosophy treatises
Policies and deployment standards
answerKey: RACI matrices
Board reporting on AI risk
Policies and deployment standards
questionBank.explanation: AI Governance commonly produces organizational artifacts such as RACI matrices, policy documents, standards, and board-level reporting. Model encryption is a cybersecurity control; ethical treatises are outputs aligned with AI Ethics but not typical governance deliverables.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: A bank’s new AI underwriting tool shows a statistically significant higher decline rate for applicants from a particular postal code. Which governance disciplines should be involved immediately? (Choose the best combination.)
options: AI Risk Management, Data Governance, Legal/Compliance, Responsible AI
IT Governance, Corporate Governance, Internal Audit
Information Governance and Cybersecurity Governance only
AI Ethics and Donor Agencies
questionBank.answerKey: AI Risk Management, Data Governance, Legal/Compliance, Responsible AI
questionBank.explanation: The issue suggests potential bias and regulatory risk, requiring risk assessment, data quality and provenance checks, legal and compliance review, and operational mitigation under Responsible AI frameworks.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Which of the following best describes the relationship between AI Compliance and AI Regulation?
options: AI Compliance creates laws that AI Regulation enforces.
AI Regulation is external rules; AI Compliance are internal activities to meet those rules.
They are interchangeable terms for the same activity.
AI Compliance only applies to contract obligations, not law.
questionBank.answerKey: AI Regulation is external rules; AI Compliance are internal activities to meet those rules.
questionBank.explanation: Regulation denotes laws and rules created by public authorities; compliance denotes the activities organizations undertake to conform with those external requirements as well as contractual obligations.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: An e-learning platform uses AI to personalize learning pathways. In a low-resource country, network outages are frequent; logging is incomplete and many students use shared devices. Which governance adaptations are most appropriate?
options: Require full-scale external audits before any further iterations.
Adopt lightweight monitoring, prioritize offline-capable features, and institute clear consent and fallback human support processes.
Stop all AI personalization until national regulation is enacted.
Outsource governance to the vendor to reduce local burden.
questionBank.answerKey: Adopt lightweight monitoring, prioritize offline-capable features, and institute clear consent and fallback human support processes.
questionBank.explanation: In resource-constrained settings, proportionate measures that focus on practical mitigation (offline capability, consent, fallback human support, simple monitoring) are more viable than heavy compliance or suspension. Outsourcing governance does not eliminate local accountability.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: You are the AI governance lead at a healthcare provider. A vendor-supplied diagnostic model performs well on aggregated metrics but shows reduced sensitivity for an ethnolinguistic minority in your community. The vendor claims the data distribution matches the training set. What is your next governance action?
options: Accept the vendor claim and continue deployment if board approves.
Require vendor to provide disaggregated performance reports, halt autonomous use for that population segment until mitigations are in place, and escalate to compliance and clinical leadership.
Disable the model for all patients to avoid reputational risk.
Remove the minority’s records from training to improve aggregate metrics.
questionBank.answerKey: Require vendor to provide disaggregated performance reports, halt autonomous use for that population segment until mitigations are in place, and escalate to compliance and clinical leadership.
questionBank.explanation: Appropriate response requires evidence from disaggregated testing, immediate risk mitigation (halt for affected group), and escalation to accountable governance actors; disabling for all is disproportionate and altering training by removing minority records harms fairness.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Select the set of governance outputs you would expect before deploying a high-risk public sector AI system.
options: Completed AI impact assessment
Model training code obfuscated with no documentation
Board-approved AI governance policy with delegated authority
Independent assurance report or plan for one
Data lineage and consent records
answerKey: Completed AI impact assessment
Board-approved AI governance policy with delegated authority
Independent assurance report or plan for one
Data lineage and consent records
questionBank.explanation: Deploying a high-risk system requires documented impact assessment, board-level governance, assurance, and data provenance. Obfuscation and lack of documentation are contrary to good governance.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: Prioritize the following controls for an AI system used for national tax auditing when resources are limited: (A) Full external audit; (B) Human-in-the-loop review for flagged cases; (C) Data provenance and lineage mapping; (D) Real-time anomaly detection for model inputs. Provide your justification.

options.rationale: Human oversight reduces immediate harms, provenance addresses root data issues, anomaly detection helps resilience; external audit is valuable but resource-intensive and can follow.
External audit should come first to ensure baseline safety.
Data provenance is foundational; then detection, then human review, then audit.

questionBank.answerKey: C, D, B, A
questionBank.explanation: Foundational measures (data provenance) should precede detection and human oversight; external audits are important but typically come after these operational controls. Learner must justify sequencing by risk-reduction impact and feasibility.

questionBank.sourceModuleTitle: AI Governance vs Related Governance Disciplines
questionBank.prompt: A multinational company is subject to new AI regulations in one jurisdiction requiring mandatory impact assessments for high-risk systems. Which coordinated response best balances compliance and operational continuity?
options: Apply the new regulated jurisdiction’s requirements globally to simplify operations.
Localize compliance—apply jurisdictional requirements to systems affecting that territory while adopting core global standards for other regions, and track differences in a compliance matrix.
Ignore the local regulation if the corporate policy is more permissive.
Outsource all compliance activities to a single external vendor to ensure uniformity.
questionBank.answerKey: Localize compliance—apply jurisdictional requirements to systems affecting that territory while adopting core global standards for other regions, and track differences in a compliance matrix.
questionBank.explanation: Local regulatory requirements should be applied where they have legal force while maintaining global baseline policies. Applying a jurisdictional requirement globally may be defensible but costly and sometimes impractical; ignoring regulation is non-compliant; outsourcing does not replace internal accountability.

questionBank.prompt: Which artifact most directly supports traceability for a deployed model?
options: A user-facing FAQ
A model registry entry with dataset and preprocessing provenance
A marketing brochure describing the system
An internal chat message
questionBank.answerKey: A model registry entry with dataset and preprocessing provenance
questionBank.explanation: Traceability requires explicit provenance records linking model versions to datasets, preprocessing and training artifacts; model registries provide this.

questionBank.prompt: Which monitoring signal would best indicate potential model drift affecting reliability?
options: Increase in the number of explanation requests
Stable training loss
Rising error rates on live data compared to validation benchmarks
Higher number of press articles
questionBank.answerKey: Rising error rates on live data compared to validation benchmarks
questionBank.explanation: Model drift manifests as degradation in live performance relative to expected benchmarks; rising error rates are a direct signal.

questionBank.prompt: What is a key trade-off when applying differential privacy to an analytics pipeline?
options: Improved explainability with no downsides
Reduced model utility in exchange for formal privacy guarantees
Increased speed of training with lower compute use
Eliminates need for access controls
questionBank.answerKey: Reduced model utility in exchange for formal privacy guarantees
questionBank.explanation: Differential privacy introduces noise which can reduce statistical utility; it provides formal privacy guarantees while impacting accuracy.

questionBank.prompt: Which control is most directly aimed at preventing poisoning of training data?
options: Differential privacy
Strong access controls and provenance checks
Providing user-facing explanations
Adding more features to model
questionBank.answerKey: Strong access controls and provenance checks
questionBank.explanation: Preventing data poisoning requires restricting data modification capabilities and verifying data provenance and integrity.

questionBank.prompt: Which principle requires providing mechanisms for affected individuals to challenge automated decisions?
options: Traceability
Contestability
Robustness
Resilience
questionBank.answerKey: Contestability
questionBank.explanation: Contestability is explicitly about providing channels and processes for appeals and challenges to automated decisions.

questionBank.prompt: Select controls that directly support accountability in an AI project (choose all that apply):
options: Assigning a named model owner
Publishing a public marketing video
Maintaining an immutable audit trail of model changes
Removing all logs after deployment
answerKey: Assigning a named model owner
Maintaining an immutable audit trail of model changes
questionBank.explanation: Accountability is enabled by clear role assignment and traceable records; marketing videos and deleting logs do not support accountability.

questionBank.prompt: A retail AI model decides promotions and is found to favor customers in a particular postal code that correlates with higher income. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Shut down all AI systems immediately
Do nothing since overall revenue increased
Suspend automated promotion targeting for that cohort pending a fairness audit and introduce manual review
Publish the model code publicly
questionBank.answerKey: Suspend automated promotion targeting for that cohort pending a fairness audit and introduce manual review
questionBank.explanation: A measured response is to suspend automated enforcement for the affected cohort, investigate through a fairness audit, and ensure human review to prevent ongoing harm while preserving operations.

questionBank.prompt: Match the following evidence types to the principle they most directly support: (A) Model card, (B) Appeal logs, (C) Penetration test report, (D) Disaggregated performance metrics.
options: A - Traceability, B - Privacy, C - Fairness, D - Security
A - Transparency, B - Contestability, C - Security, D - Fairness
A - Explainability, B - Traceability, C - Resilience, D - Accessibility
A - Accountability, B - Reliability, C - Privacy, D - Transparency
questionBank.answerKey: A - Transparency, B - Contestability, C - Security, D - Fairness
questionBank.explanation: Model cards provide transparency, appeal logs support contestability, pen test reports support security, and disaggregated metrics are used to assess fairness.

questionBank.prompt: Which monitoring indicators would you include in a post-deployment plan for a medical triage model? (select all that apply)
options: False negative rate for critical conditions
Average CPU utilization on the server
Clinician override rate
Number of user downloads of the mobile app
answerKey: False negative rate for critical conditions
Clinician override rate
questionBank.explanation: Safety-critical monitoring focuses on outcome-relevant measures (false negatives) and human override behavior; server load and app downloads are operational but not directly safety indicators.

questionBank.prompt: Which best practice reduces the risk that documentation intended for regulators inadvertently creates security vulnerability?
options: Publishing raw training data publicly
Providing summarized technical details to the public while keeping sensitive provenance under secure access for auditors
Avoiding any documentation at all
Including detailed API keys in documentation
questionBank.answerKey: Providing summarized technical details to the public while keeping sensitive provenance under secure access for auditors
questionBank.explanation: Tailored disclosure balances transparency and security by summarizing public information while granting detailed provenance access under controlled conditions to auditors.

questionBank.prompt: Advanced: You are reviewing an autonomous inspection drone network for critical infrastructure. The system uses a complex perception model. An adversarial actor crafts an input causing misdetection. Which layered strategy best reduces both the risk of successful attack and downstream harm?
options: Rely only on adversarial training of the perception model
Combine input validation, ensemble models with different architectures, sensor redundancy, robust detection thresholds, and an emergency human override pathway
Publish the entire model to crowdsource patches
Ignore the problem because physical inspection can catch issues eventually
questionBank.answerKey: Combine input validation, ensemble models with different architectures, sensor redundancy, robust detection thresholds, and an emergency human override pathway
questionBank.explanation: Defense-in-depth combining technical robustness and organizational procedures is needed for high-risk safety-critical systems; single measures are insufficient.

questionBank.prompt: Advanced: Classify the following governance responses as proactive or reactive: (A) Pre-deployment third-party fairness audit, (B) User appeal leading to model rollback, (C) Continuous monitoring dashboard, (D) Emergency patch after exploitation.
options: A - Reactive, B - Proactive, C - Reactive, D - Proactive
A - Proactive, B - Reactive, C - Proactive, D - Reactive
A - Proactive, B - Proactive, C - Reactive, D - Reactive
A - Reactive, B - Reactive, C - Proactive, D - Proactive
questionBank.answerKey: A - Proactive, B - Reactive, C - Proactive, D - Reactive
questionBank.explanation: Pre-deployment audits and monitoring seek to prevent or detect issues early (proactive); appeals and emergency patches respond to realized problems (reactive).

questionBank.prompt: Advanced: Which instruments should a public agency include in procurement to ensure vendor accountability for an AI system used in citizen services? (select all that apply)
options: Contract clauses requiring model provenance disclosure under confidentiality
No requirement for documentation to speed procurement
Right to audit and independent third-party assessment
Penalty clauses for failure to meet agreed fairness or performance SLAs
answerKey: Contract clauses requiring model provenance disclosure under confidentiality
Right to audit and independent third-party assessment
Penalty clauses for failure to meet agreed fairness or performance SLAs
questionBank.explanation: Procurement should include confidentiality-protected provenance disclosure, audit rights and enforceable performance/fairness obligations to ensure vendor compliance. Skipping documentation is inappropriate.

questionBank.prompt: Advanced: A facial recognition model has lower accuracy for a minority group but performing worse increases operational costs for safety requirements. As a governance officer, what is the defensible course of action?
options: Deploy system without mitigation since overall accuracy is high
Deploy but restrict use cases that have high risk for the affected group and require human review; schedule targeted data collection and model retraining to reduce disparity
Remove the minority group from the dataset
Ignore accuracy concerns because they are inevitable
questionBank.answerKey: Deploy but restrict use cases that have high risk for the affected group and require human review; schedule targeted data collection and model retraining to reduce disparity
questionBank.explanation: A proportional and time-bound approach balances operational needs with fairness: restrict high-risk uses, require human oversight, and commit to remediation via targeted data collection and retraining.

questionBank.prompt: A public hospital wants to deploy a clinical decision-support model. The model is accurate on a pilot dataset, but the dataset underrepresents rural patients and the explanation interface is unavailable in the dominant local language. Which governance response best converts responsible-AI principles into an actionable requirement set?
options: Approve deployment because pilot accuracy is sufficient.
Require representativeness testing and subgroup monitoring, a language-accessible explanation and review route, documented limitations, and a staged approval with post-deployment monitoring.
Reject all machine learning in healthcare regardless of risk.
Publish the model architecture but do not change the deployment process.
questionBank.answerKey: Require representativeness testing and subgroup monitoring, a language-accessible explanation and review route, documented limitations, and a staged approval with post-deployment monitoring.
questionBank.explanation: The response links inclusiveness, fairness, accessibility, transparency, contestability, proportionality and safety to requirements, controls, evidence and monitoring. Accuracy on a limited pilot does not establish trustworthy performance for the affected population.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between 'accountability' and 'responsibility'?
options: Accountability is about completing tasks; responsibility is about facing consequences.
Accountability is about facing consequences for outcomes; responsibility is about performing tasks.
Accountability and responsibility are interchangeable terms.
Responsibility always implies legal liability; accountability never does.
questionBank.answerKey: Accountability is about facing consequences for outcomes; responsibility is about performing tasks.
questionBank.explanation: Accountability concerns who is answerable for outcomes and may face sanctions; responsibility refers to duty to perform tasks. They are distinct organisational concepts.

questionBank.prompt: If a caseworker is instructed to rely on an automated recommendation but has no time to verify it, which is most likely true?
options: The caseworker is fully accountable for outcomes because they are human-in-the-loop.
The caseworker is responsible for the task but may not be accountable for the outcome.
The vendor is automatically accountable since the product generated the recommendation.
No one can be held accountable in this configuration.
questionBank.answerKey: The caseworker is responsible for the task but may not be accountable for the outcome.
questionBank.explanation: Being in the loop can indicate responsibility but, without authority, time and evidence, a human may not be held accountable for system outcomes.

questionBank.prompt: Match the term to the example: (1) Authority; (2) Ownership; (3) Liability; (4) Oversight.
options: The legal team holds the contract documents and updates them annually.
The regulator has power to impose fines for non-compliance.
The product manager can approve a production rollout.
An internal audit team reviews model performance quarterly.

answerKey.1: The product manager can approve a production rollout.
answerKey.2: The legal team holds the contract documents and updates them annually.
answerKey.3: The regulator has power to impose fines for non-compliance.
answerKey.4: An internal audit team reviews model performance quarterly.

questionBank.explanation: Authority is decision-making power, ownership is custodial responsibility, liability links to legal/regulatory exposure, and oversight is monitoring and review.

questionBank.prompt: Which element is essential to ensure answerability for a decision made by an AI system?
options: A named accountable role with access to decision evidence
A human who saw the output
A vendor disclaimer that absolves the organisation
A general policy statement
questionBank.answerKey: A named accountable role with access to decision evidence
questionBank.explanation: Answerability requires a named actor who can provide evidence and explanation; merely seeing an output or having a policy is insufficient.

questionBank.prompt: Which is the quickest way to close an immediate harm caused by a deployed recommender?
options: Renegotiating the vendor contract
Immediate rollback or disabling the recommender
Forming a committee to study the issue for three months
Publishing a statement to the public
questionBank.answerKey: Immediate rollback or disabling the recommender
questionBank.explanation: Mitigating ongoing harm requires immediate technical action (rollback/disabling) followed by investigation and communication.

questionBank.prompt: Which items should appear in the decision-rights entry for 'Approve model for production'? (Select all that apply.)
options: Required evidence bundle (validation metrics, fairness tests)
Name of Accountable role
Escalation path if tests fail
Vendor's marketing materials
answerKey: Required evidence bundle (validation metrics, fairness tests)
Name of Accountable role
Escalation path if tests fail
questionBank.explanation: Decision entries should include evidence requirements, the accountable actor, and escalation paths; vendor marketing materials are not authoritative evidence.

questionBank.prompt: A vendor contract includes a clause that the vendor is 'not liable for indirect damages' and provides no SLA on updating the model after policy changes. What governance action is most appropriate before resuming production after discovering policy misalignment?
options: Rely on vendor goodwill to patch the model
Pause the feature, renegotiate contract terms for update SLAs and require evidence of fixes
Ignore contractual issues since the vendor is external
Outsource oversight to a third-party auditor and resume production immediately
questionBank.answerKey: Pause the feature, renegotiate contract terms for update SLAs and require evidence of fixes
questionBank.explanation: Immediate pause reduces harm; contract change creates enforceable responsibilities and requires evidence of remediation.

questionBank.prompt: Match lifecycle stage to the most appropriate accountable role in a typical private-sector product team.
options: Strategy
Technical implementation
Monitoring and incident response
Procurement

answerKey.Procurement: Procurement Officer / Head of Vendor Management

questionBank.explanation: Strategy is typically owned at an executive level; technical work is owned by engineering, operations handle live monitoring, procurement handles contracts.

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following belongs in an incident playbook as the first action after detecting a high-risk model failure causing real-time harm?
options: Notify the board immediately
Execute the predefined mitigation (e.g., disable model or switch to safe baseline)
Draft a public statement
Start renegotiating vendor contracts
questionBank.answerKey: Execute the predefined mitigation (e.g., disable model or switch to safe baseline)
questionBank.explanation: Mitigating ongoing harm is the priority; communications and contractual actions follow.

questionBank.prompt: An organisation wants to avoid decision paralysis but ensure safety. Which design balances speed and control?
options: Single approver with sole authority for all changes
No approval gates, continuous deployment
Tiered approval gates where low-risk changes auto-approve and high-risk changes require committee sign-off
Every change requires full board approval
questionBank.answerKey: Tiered approval gates where low-risk changes auto-approve and high-risk changes require committee sign-off
questionBank.explanation: Tiered gates balance agility and oversight by reserving heavier controls for higher-risk changes.

questionBank.prompt: Which actions are appropriate when applying AI Governance: Purpose, Scope & Evolution in a professional governance review?
options: Define the purpose, boundaries and affected people for AI Governance: Purpose, Scope & Evolution
Assign accountable owners and decision rights
Document evidence, assumptions and review triggers
Guarantee that the system has zero risk
Delegate all governance responsibility to the vendor
answerKey: Define the purpose, boundaries and affected people for AI Governance: Purpose, Scope & Evolution
Assign accountable owners and decision rights
Document evidence, assumptions and review triggers
questionBank.explanation: A defensible governance process connects scope, accountability, evidence and review; it cannot guarantee zero risk or transfer all responsibility to a vendor.

options: Define the purpose, boundaries and affected people for Responsible & Trustworthy AI Principles

answerKey: Define the purpose, boundaries and affected people for Responsible & Trustworthy AI Principles

questionBank.prompt: Which actions are appropriate when applying Accountability, Responsibility & Decision Rights in a professional governance review?
options: Define the purpose, boundaries and affected people for Accountability, Responsibility & Decision Rights
Assign accountable owners and decision rights
